Family Health

Vulval itching and swelling: finding the cause

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Repeated itching or swelling around the vaginal opening can be uncomfortable and frustrating, particularly when it returns after treatment. Several conditions can look alike. A clear description, gentle skin care and the right examination are more useful than adding more products without knowing the cause.

Itching without discharge still needs an explanation

The vulva is the external genital area, including the labia around the vaginal opening. The vagina is the internal canal. People often call symptoms in either place “vaginal itching”, but identifying where you feel irritation helps guide an examination and treatment.

A lack of obvious discharge does not rule out thrush or another infection. Equally, itching does not automatically mean thrush: skin irritation, eczema, a longer-term skin condition or an infestation can cause similar discomfort. If treatment keeps helping briefly and symptoms return, ask for a review rather than repeating the same product indefinitely.

Contact dermatitis: a reaction to something touching the skin

Sensitive vulval skin can react to lubricants, latex condoms, laundry products, scented pads, intimate sprays, wipes, soaps, bubble bath or cleansing gels. Contact dermatitis can involve direct irritation or an allergic reaction. Itching, tenderness, redness or another change in colour, swelling, a rash or hives may follow exposure.

Pause a suspected nonessential product and use gentle care while arranging advice if symptoms persist. Improvement can take time and is not guaranteed within a few days. Keep a list of products and when you used them. If latex seems to be the problem, ask about a suitable latex-free condom that still provides STI protection; do not simply abandon protection.

Genital herpes can begin with tingling or itching

Both HSV-1 and HSV-2 can cause genital herpes. It can spread through oral, vaginal or anal sexual contact, including contact with infected skin when no sore is visible. Transmission does not require visible semen or vaginal fluid. Condoms lower risk but cannot cover every area that may shed virus.

Symptoms may include tingling or burning, blisters that open into painful sores, painful urination and, during an initial episode, fever, body aches, headache or swollen glands. Some infections are mild or unrecognised. Antiviral medicines can shorten or suppress episodes but do not remove the virus from the body. Illness or stress may coincide with recurrences. Seek assessment of new sores promptly, and tell your maternity team immediately if you are pregnant and suspect herpes.

Lichen sclerosus causes lasting changes in the skin

Lichen sclerosus can cause pale or white itchy patches, fragile skin, soreness and small cracks around the vulva or anus. It can occur at different ages and is not a sign of poor hygiene or an infection passed through sex. Its cause is not fully understood; immune processes may be involved.

A strong prescription steroid ointment is commonly used to control inflammation. The clinician should explain where, how much and how often to apply it, and how follow-up will work. Persistent symptoms may need specialist reassessment rather than an automatic switch to an immune-modifying medicine. Scarring can affect comfort and function, and a new lump, thickening or an ulcer that does not heal needs review because cancer risk is increased, although still low.

Eczema can flare on vulval skin too

Eczema may cause dryness, scaling, itching, soreness or a change in skin colour. It can affect the vulva even when there is little eczema elsewhere. Scratching can damage the surface and make symptoms harder to settle. A flare improving and later returning does not necessarily mean that you have picked up a new infection.

Triggers differ between people. Heat, sweat, irritating fabric, fragrance, detergents, stress, illness or hormonal changes can contribute. Some people have relevant allergies, but vulval itching is not a reason to eliminate broad food groups. Pregnancy or menopause may change symptoms; dryness related to lower oestrogen is another possible explanation that needs its own assessment.

Pubic lice need targeted treatment and contact care

Pubic lice can cause intense itching in hair-bearing areas. You may see tiny lice or eggs attached to hairs, scratch marks or small blue-grey marks near bites. They are usually passed through close sexual contact and can occasionally spread through shared clothing, towels or bedding. Scratching may cause secondary skin irritation or infection.

Use a product specifically appropriate for pubic lice as directed, with advice if you are pregnant, breastfeeding or treating a child. Do not apply these products near the eyes or inside the vagina. Wash and dry recently used clothing, towels and bedding as instructed, and ask how to handle items that cannot be washed. Recent sexual partners need notification and assessment or treatment; avoid sexual contact until treatment requirements are met.

Thorough whole-house disinfection or insecticide fogging is not the solution. Persistent live lice need follow-up, not repeated unsupervised chemical applications. Fever or marked fatigue should not be dismissed as routine lice symptoms. A sexual-health service can also advise about other STI checks.

Sweat and friction can keep the area irritated

Moisture trapped against the skin can worsen itching, especially with close-fitting clothes or damp exercise wear. Change out of wet clothing, choose comfortable breathable underwear and avoid garments that repeatedly rub. You do not need a special deodorant to manage normal genital scent.

After exercise, gently rinse or wash the external area and dry by patting rather than scrubbing. More washing is not always better: frequent soap use can damage an already irritated surface. If symptoms continue despite reducing heat and friction, consider another cause rather than assuming sweat explains everything.

Shaving and waxing can cause bumps and soreness

Hair removal can irritate follicles, create small cuts or lead to ingrown hairs. A shaving cream, depilatory chemical or wax can also cause a reaction. An itchy rash after hair removal may therefore be irritation, but painful blisters, spreading redness or pus should not automatically be labelled razor burn.

Pause shaving or waxing while the skin heals. If you resume, work carefully on external hair-bearing skin with clean personal equipment and a product suitable for that area; do not put hair-removal chemicals on the inner labia or inside the vagina. Trimming may be more comfortable for some people, but still needs care. Do not pick, squeeze or dig out bumps.

Keep home care simple and external

Gently cleanse the outside with lukewarm water or an emollient soap substitute recommended for you, and pat dry. Avoid douching, scented products, intimate sprays and vigorous rubbing. A plain fragrance-free emollient may protect irritated skin if suitable for the diagnosis. Choose a bland lubricant if needed and stop if it stings; check compatibility with condoms.

A clean cool damp cloth may briefly soothe itching. A comfortably warm compress may ease a minor irritated hair follicle, but avoid heat and stop if it makes symptoms worse. Loose clothing can reduce friction. Comfort measures do not treat herpes, lice or a persistent inflammatory skin condition.

Do not improvise a strong baking-soda bath or use a long soak as a general cure. Oatmeal baths may be used for some eczema care, but a household mixture is not automatically suitable for genital skin. Check with a clinician before trying bath additives. Never put these mixtures inside the vagina.

Treatment should match the diagnosis

A clinician may recommend an antifungal for confirmed or likely thrush, an antiviral for herpes, a suitable lice medicine or a prescribed steroid for a skin disorder. Antibiotics treat particular bacterial problems; they are not a general treatment for itching. Oral antihistamines can sometimes reduce itch or help sleep, but they do not remove every underlying cause and can cause drowsiness.

Hydrocortisone, stronger steroids, topical antihistamines and calamine are not interchangeable products to try on all genital symptoms. Some can irritate the skin or obscure the diagnosis. Conversely, a correctly prescribed potent steroid for lichen sclerosus is an important treatment and should not be avoided simply because the site is sensitive. Ask for clear application instructions, including pregnancy or breastfeeding precautions where relevant.

Arrange an examination when symptoms persist or change

Seek assessment for persistent or recurrent itching, white patches, blisters, ulcers, an unexplained lump, a change in skin texture or concern about an STI. Fever, severe pain, rapidly increasing swelling, spreading redness or difficulty passing urine needs urgent care. Breathing difficulty or swelling of the lips or tongue with an allergic reaction is an emergency.

The clinician may ask about discharge, skin products, medicines, sexual contact, other skin symptoms and previous treatment. With your consent they can examine the vulva and, when needed, the vagina. Swabs or other tests may help identify infection. If the diagnosis is unclear or a patch does not respond to treatment, a small skin biopsy may be suggested. Ask for a chaperone or support person if helpful and tell the clinician if you need to pause.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Absent discharge does not exclude infection, and itching alone does not establish thrush.

Skin conditions, herpes and pubic lice need different treatments; recurrent symptoms deserve review.

How BeMama can help

Bring a list of products and treatments you have used, including what improved or worsened the symptoms.

When to seek help

Get urgent help for severe swelling, fever, spreading redness or trouble passing urine. New sores during pregnancy need prompt maternity advice; breathing difficulty with an allergic reaction is an emergency.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • The vulva is external; avoid washing or treating inside the vagina without advice.
  • Keep every proposed cause open until the symptoms are assessed.
  • Prescribed steroids can be appropriate for diagnosed conditions.
  • Persistent white patches, sores or lumps should be examined.

Frequently asked questions

Can I have thrush without noticeable discharge?

Yes. Thrush can mainly irritate the vulva, but itching alone does not prove it. Other skin conditions and infections may need different treatment.

Does genital herpes only come from HSV-2?

No. Both HSV-1 and HSV-2 can cause it. Skin contact, including oral-genital contact, can transmit infection even without a visible sore.

Are white itchy patches a reason for an appointment?

Yes. Lichen sclerosus is one possible cause, but examination is needed. Persistent patches, scarring, ulcers or a new lump should not be repeatedly treated as thrush.

Are strong steroid ointments always unsafe on the vulva?

No. A prescribed potent steroid can be essential for conditions such as lichen sclerosus. Follow the exact site, amount and schedule instead of applying an unselected product.

Must I disinfect my whole home for pubic lice?

No. Use appropriate treatment and targeted care of recently used clothes, towels and bedding, with partner management. Whole-house insecticide treatment is unnecessary.

Should I wash more often to stop the itching?

Overwashing can worsen irritation. Gentle external cleansing and drying are preferable to frequent soap, scrubbing, scented wipes or douching.

Can I use a baking-soda bath as a cure?

Do not use a strong household mixture as a general genital treatment. Bath additives can irritate, and soothing the skin does not treat every cause. Ask for advice specific to the diagnosis.

Should I stop eating certain foods for vulval eczema?

Not routinely. Triggers vary, and broad food restriction is not a substitute for assessment. Discuss a suspected allergy before making nutritional changes.

Can shaving explain every itchy bump?

No. Shaving may irritate follicles or cause ingrown hairs, but infection or herpes can look similar. Stop hair removal and seek advice for blisters, pus, spreading redness or persistent symptoms.

Will I definitely need a biopsy?

No. History, examination and sometimes swabs may identify the cause. A biopsy can be useful when the diagnosis is uncertain, the skin has concerning changes or treatment is not working.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
